title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Proportion
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.4 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
intro: After this lesson you can interpret an interval and its confidence level, say what changes the width of an interval, decide whether an interval supports a claim, and find the sample size for a target margin of error.

moments.title: What this lesson adds
moments.text: Interpreting an interval, interpreting the confidence level, the effect of confidence and sample size, justifying claims, and sample size for a target margin.

moments.title: Utah governor's poll
moments.text: 180 of 345 registered voters say they will vote for her, and she builds a 95% interval.

moments.title: Interpret the interval
moments.text: State the confidence level, both endpoints, and the parameter in context.

moments.title: If the truth is outside the interval
moments.text: Then the sample was one of the unusual 5%, extremely high or low.

moments.title: Either in the interval or not
moments.text: The true proportion is either in your interval or it is not, and you cannot tell which.

moments.title: Confident is not a probability
moments.text: Do not say there is a 95% chance that $p$ is in the interval.

moments.title: Interpret the confidence level
moments.text: In repeated random sampling with the same $n$, about $C$% of the intervals capture $p$.

moments.title: Many intervals
moments.text: Intervals from many samples: most catch the true proportion and about 5% miss.

moments.title: More confidence, wider interval
moments.text: A higher level raises $z^*$ and the margin of error, so the interval is wider and less precise.

moments.title: Bigger sample, smaller margin
moments.text: $n$ is in the denominator of the standard error, so a larger $n$ shrinks the margin of error.

moments.title: Does the governor have evidence?
moments.text: (0.469, 0.575) contains 0.50 and values below it, so it does not show she gets more than 50%.

moments.title: A different interval
moments.text: If the interval were (0.524, 0.604), the whole interval is above 0.50, which supports her claim.

moments.title: Solve for the sample size
moments.text: Start from a desired margin of error and solve the margin-of-error formula for $n$.

moments.title: Choosing $\hat p$ before sampling
moments.text: Use a proportion from a previous study, or 0.5 when you have no idea.

moments.title: Tax poll, margin 0.03 at 95%
moments.text: With $\hat p=0.5$ the sample size is about 1,067, rounded up to 1,068.

moments.title: Self-checkout, margin 0.04 at 90%
moments.text: Using 42% from a previous study, about 412 customers.

moments.title: Undergraduate part-time jobs
moments.text: A 90% interval of (0.31, 0.39) from 400 students. Interpret it, interpret the level, and judge two claims.

moments.title: Dean versus president
moments.text: The whole interval is below 40%, so it supports the dean. It includes 36%, so it does not support the president.

sections.title: Does the interval support the claim?

cards.name: Convincing evidence
cards.text: Every value in the interval is on the side of the claim.

cards.name: Not convincing
cards.text: The interval contains the claimed boundary value or values on both sides of it.

Governor, if the interval had been

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video says the governor "might" win and "might" lose. On the exam, write that the interval does not provide convincing evidence for the claim because it includes 0.50 and values below it. Do not argue from how many values sit on each side of 0.50.

cards.name: Confidence level
cards.text: Higher level means larger $z^*$, so a wider interval.

cards.name: Sample size
cards.text: Larger $n$ means a smaller standard error, so a narrower interval.

cells: Raise the level and also take a larger sample

sections.title: Choose a sample size for a target margin of error
sections.intro: Researchers often start with the margin of error they want and solve for $n$. Solve $\text{ME}=z^*\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ for $n$.
steps: Write down the margin of error ME you want.
Choose $\hat p$ before sampling: use a proportion from a previous study if the problem gives one, otherwise use 0.5.
Round up to the next whole number.

parts.label: No prior information
parts.text: Gives the largest $n$, so the margin of error is guaranteed.

parts.label: Prior study
parts.text: Use the earlier proportion when the problem gives it.

sections.title: Interval capture explorer
sections.intro: Draw several batches of 100 intervals. Compare 90%, 95% and 99%, and then raise $n$. A higher level catches more but gives wider intervals, and a larger $n$ gives narrower ones. Even at 99%, about 1 interval in 100 misses.

stories.gov: Suppose 52% of Utah's registered voters would vote for the governor. Each poll surveys 345 randomly chosen voters, and each gives its own interval for $p$.
stories.gov4: Same voters, but each poll surveys 1,380 voters, four times as many.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Work through each task in it yourself, the way you would on the exam, then check what you observe.

steps.title: Critical value for 90%
steps.how: tap the plus button, choose Inference, then Probability Distributions, then Normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Open Cumulative Probability, switch from area to bounds, choose the inner option and enter 0.90.
steps.observe: The bounds are $\pm$ the same number. Repeat with 0.95 and 0.99 and compare.

steps.title: Sample size with no prior information
steps.suppose: we want $n$ for a margin of error of 0.03 at 95% confidence, with no prior proportion.
steps.observe: The calculator shows 1067.1. A sample of 1,067 would give a margin just above 0.03, so round up.

steps.title: Sample size with a previous study
steps.suppose: we want $n$ for a margin of error of 0.04 at 90% confidence, given that a previous study found 42%.
steps.observe: The result is 412.0. Compare it with the no-prior answer for the same margin: using 0.5 would need more.

steps.title: The governor's interval
steps.suppose: we want the 95% interval for 180 of 345 voters, to check the claim that she gets more than 50%.
steps.how: tap the plus button, choose Inference, then the $z$ test for proportions. Enter 180 successes and 345 for the sample size, create the test and open the confidence interval.
steps.observe: Check whether 0.50 is inside the interval. If it is, the interval does not provide convincing evidence for the claim.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Calling confidence a probability
traps.weak: There is a 95% probability that the true proportion is between 0.469 and 0.574.
traps.better: I am 95% confident that the proportion of all registered voters in Utah who will vote for the governor is between 46.9% and 57.4%.

traps.title: Interpreting the confidence level
traps.weak: 95% of the time, the true proportion is in 0.469 to 0.574.
traps.better: If many random samples of 345 registered voters in Utah were taken, about 95% of the intervals constructed this way would capture the true proportion who will vote for the governor.

traps.title: Counting values on each side of the claim
traps.weak: There are more values above 0.50 than below, so she will win.
traps.better: The interval includes 0.50 and values below it, so it does not provide convincing evidence that more than 50% of voters will vote for her.

traps.title: Treating a higher level as a free upgrade
traps.weak: A 99% interval is better because it is more confident.
traps.better: A 99% interval has a larger $z^*$, so it is wider and less precise. To keep it narrow, increase the sample size.

traps.title: Rounding the sample size to the nearest whole number
traps.better: Round up. $n=1,068$ guarantees a margin of error of at most 0.03, while 1,067 falls just short.

questions.stem: A 90% confidence interval for a population proportion is calculated from a random sample. Which statement correctly interprets the 90% confidence level?
opts: There is a 90% probability that the true proportion is in this interval
90% of the population is in this interval
In repeated random samples of the same size, about 90% of the intervals made this way would capture the true proportion
The sample proportion is within 90% of the true proportion
why: Once the interval is computed, the true proportion either is in it or is not.
The interval estimates a proportion, not a share of the population.
The level describes the long-run capture rate of the method across many samples.
The level is not about how close $\hat p$ is to $p$ in percentage terms.

questions.stem: All else equal, the sample size for a 95% interval is increased from 400 to 1,600. What happens to the margin of error?
opts: It is cut to one quarter
why: A larger sample makes the margin smaller.
$n$ is under a square root, so quadrupling $n$ cuts the standard error and the margin of error in half.
It would be one quarter only if $n$ were not under a square root.
The margin of error depends on $n$.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a proportion of residents who support a plan is (0.58, 0.66). Does it provide convincing evidence for the claim that more than 55% support it?
opts: Yes, because every value in the interval is greater than 0.55
No, because the interval is wider than 0.05
No, because the midpoint 0.62 is not 0.55
why: The lowest plausible value, 0.58, is still above 0.55.
Width does not matter. What matters is whether 0.55 is in the interval.
The midpoint is the point estimate. The claim is judged by the whole interval.
One endpoint being above 0.55 is not enough. The whole interval must be.

questions.stem: No prior information is available. About how large a sample is needed for a 95% confidence interval with a margin of error of at most 0.05?
why: This is $z^*/\text{ME}=1.96/0.05$ without squaring or multiplying by $\hat p(1-\hat p)$.
$0.5(0.5)(1.96/0.05)^2=384.16$. Rounding down to 384 would give a margin just over 0.05.
This doubles the correct value.
$n=384.16$, so round up to 385.

questions.stem: Which change would make a confidence interval for a proportion narrower?
opts: Raising the confidence level from 95% to 99%
Using a sample proportion closer to 0.5
why: A higher level increases $z^*$ and widens the interval.
A larger $n$ decreases the standard error and the margin of error.
A smaller $n$ increases the standard error.
$\hat p(1-\hat p)$ is largest at 0.5, which makes the standard error larger, not smaller.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A principal wants to estimate the proportion of students at her school who walk to school. A random sample of 200 students gives a 90% confidence interval of (0.19, 0.29).
parts: (c) A school board member claims that fewer than 35% of students walk. Does the interval provide convincing evidence for the claim? Justify your answer.
(d) The principal plans a new random sample with a margin of error of at most 0.02 at 95% confidence. Using the sample proportion from this interval, find the sample size needed.
sample: (a) I am 90% confident that the proportion of all students at this school who walk to school is between 0.19 and 0.29.
(b) If many random samples of 200 students were taken, about 90% of the intervals constructed this way would capture the true proportion of students who walk to school.
(c) Yes. Every value in the interval is below 0.35, so the interval provides convincing evidence that fewer than 35% of students walk to school.
(d) The sample proportion is the midpoint, $\hat p=0.24$. $n=0.24(0.76)\left(\dfrac{1.96}{0.02}\right)^2\approx1751.8$, so the principal needs at least 1,752 students.
checklist: (a) Confidence level, both endpoints and the parameter in context
(b) Repeated random samples of 200 and about 90% of the intervals capture the proportion
(b) Does not refer to this one interval
(c) Notes the whole interval is below 0.35 and concludes the claim is supported
